title: 161. Quantitative Relationships & Measurement: Checking Units in Quantitative Claims
description: A comprehensive mathematics curriculum progressing from foundational numeracy and core mathematical concepts to algebra, geometry, calculus, linear algebra, probability, statistics, discrete mathematics, optimization, mathematical foundations of AI, advanced pure mathematics, and emerging research methods.

questions.learningObjective: Determine whether a stated unit is appropriate for a speed claim.
questions.question: A student claims that a car's speed is \(60\text{ meters}\). Is this claim dimensionally correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Yes, because meters measure distance.

options.label: B
options.text: No, because speed must be expressed as distance per unit time.

questions.explanation: Speed describes how much distance is covered per unit time. Its unit must therefore combine distance and time, such as meters per second or kilometers per hour. Meters alone measure distance, not speed. Therefore, the claim is not dimensionally correct, so B is correct.
questions.hint: Ask what quantity speed measures and how its unit must be formed.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the correct unit for density in a quantitative claim.
questions.question: Which unit is appropriate for density?

options.label: A
options.text: \(\text{kg/m}^3\)

options.label: B
options.text: \(\text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^3\)

questions.explanation: Density is mass divided by volume. The unit is therefore a mass unit divided by a volume unit, such as kilograms per cubic meter, \(\text{kg/m}^3\). The option \(\text{kg}\cdot\text{m}^3\) multiplies mass by volume, which is not density. Therefore, A is correct.
questions.hint: Recall that density equals mass divided by volume.

questions.concept: Unit Conversion in a Distance Claim
questions.learningObjective: Check whether a kilometer-to-meter conversion in a claim is correct.
questions.question: A runner completes \(2.5\text{ km}\). A claim states that this distance is \(2500\text{ m}\). Is the claim correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Yes, because \(1\text{ km}=1000\text{ m}\), so \(2.5\text{ km}=2500\text{ m}\).

options.label: B
options.text: No, because \(2.5\text{ km}=250\text{ m}\).

questions.explanation: Since \(1\text{ km}=1000\text{ m}\), multiply \(2.5\times 1000=2500\). Thus \(2.5\text{ km}\) equals \(2500\text{ m}\). The claim is correct, so A is correct.
questions.hint: Use the conversion factor \(1\text{ km}=1000\text{ m}\).

questions.concept: Unit Checking in an Average Speed Calculation
questions.learningObjective: Verify the unit of an average speed obtained by division.
questions.question: A car travels \(150\text{ km}\) in \(2\text{ h}\). A claim states that its average speed is \(75\text{ km/h}\). Is the claim correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Yes, because \(150\div 2=75\), and the unit is \(\text{km/h}\).

options.label: B
options.text: No, because the unit of speed should be \(\text{h/km}\).

questions.explanation: Average speed is distance divided by time. Here, \(150\text{ km}\div 2\text{ h}=75\text{ km/h}\). The numerical value and the unit are both correct. Therefore, A is correct.
questions.hint: Check both the division and the resulting unit.

questions.learningObjective: Identify an incorrect area unit in a geometric claim.
questions.question: A rectangular floor is \(5\text{ m}\) long and \(3\text{ m}\) wide. A claim states that its area is \(15\text{ m}\). Is the claim correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Yes, because \(5\times 3=15\).

options.label: B
options.text: No, because the area unit should be \(\text{m}^2\), not \(\text{m}\).

questions.explanation: Area is found by multiplying length by width: \(5\text{ m}\times 3\text{ m}=15\text{ m}^2\). The numerical value \(15\) is correct, but the unit should be square meters. Therefore, the claim as written is not correct, so B is correct.
questions.hint: When multiplying two lengths, determine the resulting unit.

questions.learningObjective: Verify the unit of work in a force-distance claim.
questions.question: A force of \(10\text{ N}\) acts over a distance of \(2\text{ m}\). A claim states that the work done is \(20\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}\). Is the unit in the claim correct?

options.label: A
options.text: No, because work should have the unit \(\text{N/m}\).

options.label: B
options.text: Yes, because work equals force times distance, so its unit is \(\text{N}\cdot\text{m}\).

questions.explanation: Work is calculated as force multiplied by distance. The unit is therefore \(\text{N}\cdot\text{m}\), which is also called the joule. Here, \(10\text{ N}\times 2\text{ m}=20\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}\). Therefore, the unit in the claim is correct, so B is correct.
questions.hint: Recall the formula for work and multiply the units.

questions.learningObjective: Check whether a pressure unit matches the definition force per area.
questions.question: Pressure is defined as force divided by area. A claim states that pressure can be measured in \(\text{N/m}^2\). Is the claim correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Yes, because pressure is force per area, so its unit is \(\text{N/m}^2\).

options.label: B
options.text: No, because pressure should have the unit \(\text{N}\cdot\text{m}^2\).

questions.explanation: Pressure equals force divided by area. Dividing the unit of force by the unit of area gives \(\text{N/m}^2\). Therefore, the claimed unit is correct, so A is correct.
questions.hint: Divide the unit of force by the unit of area.

questions.concept: Unit Checking in a Concentration Claim
questions.learningObjective: Verify the unit of concentration obtained by dividing mass by volume.
questions.question: A solution is made by dissolving \(5\text{ g}\) of salt in \(2\text{ L}\) of water. A claim states that the concentration is \(2.5\text{ g/L}\). Is the claim correct?

options.label: A
options.text: No, because the concentration should be \(0.4\text{ g/L}\).

options.label: B
options.text: Yes, because \(5\div 2=2.5\), and the unit is \(\text{g/L}\).

questions.explanation: Concentration is mass divided by volume. Here, \(5\text{ g}\div 2\text{ L}=2.5\text{ g/L}\). Both the numerical value and the unit are correct. Therefore, B is correct.
questions.hint: Divide the mass by the volume and keep the resulting unit.

questions.concept: Unit of Speed from Distance and Time
questions.learningObjective: Identify an incorrect speed unit in a division claim.
questions.question: A student calculates \(120\text{ km}\div 1.5\text{ h}=80\), and then writes the speed as \(80\text{ h/km}\). Is the stated unit correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Yes, because the calculation gives \(80\).

options.label: B
options.text: No, because speed should have the unit \(\text{km/h}\), not \(\text{h/km}\).

questions.explanation: The numerical value \(120\div 1.5=80\) is correct. However, speed is distance divided by time, so the unit must be \(\text{km/h}\). Writing \(\text{h/km}\) reverses the relationship. Therefore, the stated unit is incorrect, so B is correct.
questions.hint: Check the order of distance and time in the unit.

questions.concept: Unit Consistency in Fuel Consumption Claims
questions.learningObjective: Use a rate with units to verify the unit of a calculated fuel amount.
questions.question: A car uses \(8\text{ L}\) of fuel per \(100\text{ km}\). A claim states that the car will use \(20\text{ L}\) of fuel to travel \(250\text{ km}\). Is the claim correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Yes, because \(\frac{8}{100}\times 250=20\), and the result is in liters.

options.label: B
options.text: No, because the result should be \(32\text{ L}\), since \(8\times 4=32\).

questions.explanation:
The fuel consumption rate is \(\frac{8\text{ L}}{100\text{ km}}\). To find the fuel for \(250\text{ km}\), compute:
\[
\frac{8\text{ L}}{100\text{ km}}\times 250\text{ km}=20\text{ L}
\]
The kilometers cancel, leaving liters. Therefore, the claim is correct, so A is correct.
questions.hint: Multiply the rate by the distance and check that the remaining unit is liters.
